opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that they're going to become much harder to separate. For a long time we treated the model as the engine and the interface as the dashboard bolted onto the front. But with these systems, the behavior of the model *is* a large part of the user experience, and the interface shapes what behavior people even ask for.

One thing I'm excited about comes out of the interpretability work Fernanda and I have been doing. If you look inside these models, you find they're often building internal representations of the conversation, including, in some cases, a kind of model of the user: guesses about things like who you are, what you know, what you want. Right now that's completely invisible. You just get text back, and you have no idea what assumptions shaped it. So one direction I find really compelling is interfaces that surface some of that internal state, almost like a dashboard showing "here's what the system thinks is going on," and maybe even letting you adjust it. If the model has decided you're a beginner, or that you want a terse answer, you could see that and correct it.

That changes the relationship. Instead of model behavior being something you poke at indirectly through prompting, it becomes something you can perceive and steer more directly. I think that's healthier, both for usability and for trust, because a lot of the frustration and some of the risk with these systems comes from that opacity.

More broadly, I think the chat box is a very early form. It's a bit like the command line: incredibly flexible, but it puts the burden on the user to know what to type. Over time I'd expect interfaces to become more visual and more situated, where the model's capabilities are expressed through richer controls, and where the model in turn learns to behave in ways that fit those interfaces. So it's really co-evolution: design will push on what behavior we train for, and new model capabilities will open up design possibilities we can't quite imagine yet.

r001.rationale: The response proposes surfacing the model’s assumptions and letting users adjust or correct them, connecting that visibility to trust and reducing risks from opacity.

r002.rationale: It says interface design should shape the behavior models are trained for, and that models should learn to behave in ways that fit those interfaces.

r003.rationale: It describes co-evolution in both directions: design influences trained behavior, while new model capabilities open up new design possibilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that's become clear to me over the last few years is that you can't really separate those two anymore. For a long time, interface design was about taking a fixed system, something with known behavior, and figuring out how to expose it to people in a way that made sense. The model was the engine and the interface was the dashboard. But with these large models, the behavior itself is malleable in a way we've never had before. You can shape it with the prompt, with fine-tuning, with the way you structure the context. So the interface designer is now, in some sense, also designing the behavior, and the people shaping the behavior are making interface decisions whether they realize it or not.

One concrete way I think about it comes out of the interpretability work we've been doing. When you look inside these models, you find they're often tracking things about the user, their state, the situation, that never show up in the output. The model may have an internal estimate of whether you're an expert or a novice, or whether you're frustrated. Right now that's completely invisible. And I think one of the big opportunities in interface design is to surface some of that, to give people a window into what the system thinks is going on. Partly that's about trust, because people are much more comfortable with a system when they can see its assumptions. But it's also about control. If I can see the model has decided I'm a beginner, I can correct that, and the interaction gets better immediately.

The flip side is that I'm wary of the chat box becoming the only paradigm. Chat is wonderful for some things, but it's a very narrow channel. Humans are visual, spatial creatures. We've spent decades learning how to build direct manipulation interfaces, where you see the state of something and act on it, and I'd hate to throw that away because a text box is the easiest thing to put in front of a model. So I expect we'll see hybrids, where the model is the thing generating the interface or adapting it on the fly, and the conversation is one mode among several.

And then there's a feedback loop in the other direction. The way people interact with these systems becomes training data, implicitly or explicitly. So interface decisions, like what you make easy to say, what you make easy to correct, end up shaping future model behavior. That's a pretty heavy responsibility for designers, and I don't think the field has fully internalized it yet. My hope is that we get much more experimental about it, with lots of small, honest studies about what actually helps people, rather than assuming we already know what the interface for AI should look like.

r001.rationale: The response says users should be able to see the model’s assumptions and correct them, linking transparency to control when its assumptions are wrong.

r002.rationale: It describes shaping model behavior through prompts, fine-tuning, and context structure to improve the interaction and user experience.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a feedback loop: interface choices shape user interactions, which become training data and influence future model behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re going to evolve together quite closely. The interface shapes what people ask a model to do, and then the model’s behavior changes what kinds of interfaces are useful. If you start with a chat box, you get a conversation. But that’s not necessarily the best way to explore a large collection of information, or compare several possibilities, or understand what changed between two versions of something.

One direction I’m interested in is giving people something they can see and manipulate alongside the conversation. You might have a visualization that lets you notice a pattern, ask a question about it, and then check the answer against the underlying data. The model can help guide that exploration, but the person still has a way to examine what’s going on.

And there’s a feedback loop there. As you build those interfaces, you discover that you need particular behaviors from the model—maybe it needs to ask a clarifying question, or make a small, precise change instead of generating everything again. So I don’t think it’s simply a matter of models getting better and designers putting a nicer wrapper around them. Designing the interaction helps us figure out what ‘better’ should mean.

r001.rationale: The response says users can examine the underlying data and manipulate a visualization, but it does not clearly pair transparency with a way to intervene when problems arise.

r002.rationale: It says interface design reveals needed model behaviors, such as asking clarifying questions or making precise changes, to support the interaction.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a feedback loop: interfaces reveal needed model behaviors, and those behaviors shape useful interfaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ll evolve in a feedback loop. You build an interface around what a model can do, and then watching people use it reveals both capabilities you hadn’t anticipated and limitations that weren’t obvious in a benchmark. That changes what you want from the next model, which opens up new interface possibilities.

One interesting question is how much of the interaction should be a conversation. Language is wonderfully flexible, but sometimes you want to point at something, compare two alternatives side by side, or directly change one part of a result. I suspect we’ll see more combinations of conversation and direct manipulation.

And as models become more capable, helping people understand and steer them becomes more important. A good interface should give you ways to explore what the model is doing, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover. To me, that makes interface design part of developing the model, rather than something you add at the end.

r001.rationale: It says interfaces should help people recognize when something has gone wrong and recover, providing a way to intervene.

r002.rationale: It explains that observing how people use an interface changes what capabilities are wanted from the next model, connecting model behavior to the desired experience.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a feedback loop in which model capabilities shape the interface and user interactions inform what is wanted from the next model.
